title: Baseline retest for cores/bench
EX critical-path surgery: multi-cycle mul/div unit + five measured path cuts (5.4 -> ~70+ MHz)
motivation:
Baseline Fmax is 5.44 MHz: the worst path (199.8 ns, 156 cells) is
forward_unit -> ex_stage -> alu -> dmem address, i.e. the single-cycle
combinational `/` and `%` in alu.sv. CoreMark runs almost no DIV/REM and
only ~4-5% MULs, so every instruction pays a 200 ns clock for an
operation it does not use. Fitness = iter/cycle x Fmax, so this is worth
an order of magnitude.

I measured the chain of next-limiting paths with Gowin (`make timing
TARGET=bench`, placement option 0), stubbing M-ops with the ALTOPS
formulas to model "M-unit off the single-cycle path". Cumulative Fmax:
  baseline                                              5.44 MHz
  1. DIV/REM off the EX path                           46.6 MHz
  2. + redirect no longer muxes the instr into hazard  51.7 MHz
  3. + MUL off the EX path                             59.6 MHz
  4. + dedicated rs1+imm data-address adder            61.3 MHz
  5. + forwarding selects precomputed in ID            69.2 MHz
  6. + regfile as distributed RAM (not BSRAM)          75.9 MHz
  7. + WB data pre-muxed in MEM                        78.1 MHz
Steps 2 and 4-7 do not change cycle counts; only the M-unit costs IPC
(+1 cycle per MUL, ~3%; DIV/REM are rare).
Verification status of the probes: steps 2 and 4-7 (B-F below) applied
on top of the unmodified combinational ALU pass `make cosim` (selftest +
CoreMark RVFI diff vs the ISS). They have NOT been run through formal,
and the M-unit (A) was only modelled by stubs, not implemented.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Bundle of local EX-path micro-optimisations, no change in pipeline depth.

A. Sequential M-unit (new rtl/muldiv.sv), M-op waits in EX until done.
   - Divider: one shared radix-2 restoring divider, 32 iterations, on
     |a|,|b| with sign fix-up; RV32M corner cases: x/0 -> all ones (do
     not negate the quotient when b==0), rem by 0 -> dividend,
     INT_MIN/-1 -> INT_MIN, rem 0.
   - Multiplier: ONE 33x33 signed multiply (operands sign/zero-extended
     per MUL/MULH/MULHSU/MULHU) instead of three 64-bit ones. Operands
     are registered on the first EX cycle, the product (hi/lo select) is
     written to EX/MEM on the second: MUL = 2 EX cycles, DSP path is
     reg -> DSP -> reg.
   - New `ex_busy` to hazard_unit: PC and ID/EX hold; EX/MEM takes a
     bubble (valid=0, all ctrl=0) unless dmem_stall holds it. The unit
     latches the post-forwarding operands on its first EX cycle (the
     forwarding sources drain while it waits), keeps iterating during
     dmem_stall, and holds `done` until EX/MEM accepts. RVFI
     rs1/rs2_rdata of the M-op come from the latched operands.
   - Under RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS the unit returns the same XOR stand-ins
     through the same handshake with 1 extra cycle, so BMC depth still
     covers M-op stall/forwarding. alu.sv keeps only RV32I ops.
B. if_stage: out.instr = raw imem_data (no NOP mux on redirect/flush).
   Bubbles are made by the ID/EX synchronous clear instead:
   flush_id = (load_use || redirect || imem_stall) && !dmem_stall.
   Equivalent: redirect already overrides stall on the PC and clears
   ID/EX; a spurious load_use from garbage/wrong-path bits only happens
   in cycles that are bubbled anyway. Cuts branch-compare -> redirect ->
   instr mux -> rs addr -> load_use -> ID/EX (was the 26.8 ns path).
C. Dedicated address adder: new EX/MEM field mem_addr <= rs1 + imm
   (post-forward). mem_stage uses it for dmem_addr, byte mask, misalign
   and load shift. Gowin absorbs the dmem address register into the
   bench BSRAM, so today the whole ALU result mux sits in front of the
   BSRAM address pins; after this only fwd-mux + adder does.
D. Precompute forwarding in ID: ID/EX carries 4 match bits (rs1/rs2 ==
   rd of the instr now in ID/EX resp. EX/MEM, rd != 0, reg_write). In EX
   sel = (m_ex & EX/MEM.reg_write) ? 1 : (m_mem & MEM/WB.reg_write) ? 2
   : 0, which keeps the late trap gating of reg_write and the
   hold_mem_wb forwarding during dmem_stall. Removes two 5-bit
   comparators + priority from the head of every EX path.
E. Regfile as distributed RAM (`syn_ramstyle = "distributed_ram"`, no
   reset loop over the array; keep reads-as-zero after reset via x0 mux
   plus `initial` zeroing or a 32-bit written mask). Today Gowin folds
   the array plus ID/EX rs1_val/rs2_val into BSRAM, so every EX path
   starts with a 2.26 ns BSRAM clk-to-out and a bypass mux; with LUT-RAM
   the read is in ID and EX starts from plain flops.
F. MEM/WB stores one pre-muxed rd value (mem_to_reg ? load_data :
   alu_result); wb_stage and the MEM/WB forwarding source become a plain
   register output.

Expected: ~65-78 MHz at ~0.97x baseline iter/cycle, i.e. fitness
roughly 140-165 vs 12.12 (well beyond the +50 the schema field allows).

title: Multi-cycle M unit: iterative divider + registered DSP multiplier, EX-stage stall
motivation:
Fmax is 5.44 MHz because of one path: 199.8 ns, 156 logic cells,
MEM/WB.rd > u_fwd > u_ex > u_alu > EX/MEM.alu_result (whose D input Gowin
has merged into the dmem BSRAM address register). That path is the
single-cycle combinational divider: alu.sv instantiates FOUR 32-bit
divide/modulo operators (signed /, unsigned /, signed %, unsigned %) plus
three 64-bit multipliers, all behind the forwarding muxes. It also makes
the core 12312 LUT4 (target 10000).

Measured with the Python ISS on the fitness binary (coremark.elf, between
the 0x10000100/0x10000104 markers): 2,922,016 retired instructions, of
which 93,960 are MUL (3.2%) and ZERO are DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU/MULH*. The
baseline spends 4,491,485 cycles there. So every instruction pays a
200 ns clock for a divider CoreMark never uses in the timed region, and
making M ops multi-cycle costs almost nothing in cycles: each extra
MUL cycle is +2.1% cycles, and divide latency is free.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move MUL*/DIV*/REM* out of the combinational ALU into a sequential M unit
(new rtl/muldiv.sv) that holds the instruction in EX until its result is
ready. alu.sv keeps only add/sub/logic/shift/compare/LUI.

M unit:
  - Operands are LATCHED from the post-forwarding rs1/rs2 muxes on the
    first EX cycle of the M op. This is mandatory, not an optimisation:
    while the op waits in EX the producers drain out of EX/MEM and MEM/WB,
    so the live forwarding muxes go stale. The result AND the
    EX/MEM.rs1_val/rs2_val (RVFI rs*_rdata) must come from the latched
    copies.
  - Multiply: ONE shared 33x33 signed multiplier (operands sign- or
    zero-extended to 33 bits per MUL/MULH/MULHSU/MULHU) replacing the
    three 64-bit ones, with registered operands and a registered product
    so the DSP blocks sit flop-to-flop: MUL spends 3 cycles in EX
    (2 extra, about +4.2% cycles). Low/high half selected from the
    product register.
  - Divide: ONE shared radix-2 restoring divider on magnitudes, 1 bit per
    cycle (latch + 32 iterations + sign fix-up, ~34 cycles; no early-out
    needed since the timed region has no divides). RV32M corner cases:
    divisor 0 gives quotient all-ones (suppress the sign negation) and
    remainder = dividend; INT_MIN/-1 falls out of the magnitude datapath
    (q=0x80000000, r=0).
  - Under `ifdef RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS the SAME start/busy/done FSM is used
    but the result is the existing ALTOPS formula applied to the latched
    operands with a short fixed latency (same as MUL) for every M op, so
    the depth-20 insn BMC and the liveness check still see M ops retire
    (PicoRV32 does the same). The real and ALTOPS branches stay
    consistent with the riscv-formal insn models.

Pipeline control:
  - ex_busy = ID/EX holds a valid M op whose result is not ready. It must
    be a function of flops only (ID/EX.ctrl.is_muldiv, ID/EX.valid, FSM
    state), never of the forwarding/ALU datapath, so the stall network
    does not become the new critical path.
  - While ex_busy: PC and ID/EX hold (stall_if/stall_id, no flush),
    EX/MEM captures a bubble (valid=0, reg_write=0, mem_read/mem_write=0)
    unless dmem_stall is holding it. When done, the result is held until
    EX/MEM actually accepts it (dmem_stall may still be asserted), then
    the unit returns to idle; back-to-back M ops must restart cleanly.
  - An M op never redirects, so redirect/flush priority is unchanged; a
    wrong-path M op is squashed in ID/EX before it can start because
    flush_id clears the register in the redirect cycle.

Expected result: EX critical path shrinks to forward-mux > 32-bit
adder/shifter > EX/MEM (roughly 15-25 ns instead of 200 ns), i.e. Fmax
around 40-65 MHz, at ~4% more cycles (4.49M -> ~4.68M). Fitness should
rise from 12 to roughly 80-130 iter/s, and LUT4 should drop to a few
thousand. The +50 below is the schema ceiling, not the estimate.

title: Zero-bubble fetch-cycle branch prediction: bimodal direction + JAL folding + return stack
motivation:
The core has no branch prediction: every taken branch, JAL and JALR is
resolved in EX and squashes the fetch slot behind it. IF and ID share
one cycle here, so the penalty is exactly 1 cycle per taken control
transfer. Measured on the baseline RTL (retire trace of the scored
CoreMark run, --istall --dstall): 2.94M instructions, CPI 1.537,
18.1% branches (55.6% taken), 49.6k JAL, 13.8k JALR (13,772 of them
returns). That is 359k redirects = 7.96% of all cycles spent on
redirect bubbles.
Fmax is pinned at 5.4 MHz by the 200 ns forward->ALU (combinational
divide) path with ~150 logic levels, so logic added to the fetch cycle
and to the redirect compare is nowhere near critical: iterations/cycle
gained by prediction converts directly into fitness.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Because imem data arrives in the same cycle as the PC and IF/ID is
combinational, the real decoder + imm_gen outputs for the instruction
being fetched are known before the PC register's next state is chosen.
Use them to steer the PC in the fetch cycle itself - no BTB, and zero
bubbles on a correct prediction:
  * JAL: always predicted taken, pred target = pc + J-imm.
  * Conditional branch: direction from a 1024-entry table of 2-bit
    saturating counters indexed by pc[11:2] (async read); target =
    pc + B-imm. Trained in EX when the branch leaves EX (index
    recomputed from the ID/EX pc; train once, not on every held cycle).
  * JALR with rs1 in {x1,x5} and rd not in {x1,x5} (a return): target =
    top of an 8-entry return-address stack; JAL/JALR with rd in
    {x1,x5} push pc+4. Other JALRs: predict pc+4 (as today).
  * Never predict a target with bit 1 set, so PC stays word-aligned and
    the existing misalign-trap behaviour is untouched.
The predicted next PC (pred_npc) is captured in ID/EX with the
instruction. EX keeps computing the architectural next PC exactly as
today (the pc_next mux, including misalign fall-through to pc+4) and

redirect_target = actual_npc. The predictor is therefore a pure hint:
any wrong or uninitialised prediction is repaired by the same 1-cycle
redirect the core already has, and RVFI pc_wdata still comes from the
architectural value, so the formal contract is unchanged.

a redirect squashes the only wrong-path fetch in the same cycle, so no
wrong-path instruction is ever consumed; RAS push/pop done only on
consume therefore never needs checkpoint or repair.

backward-taken +5.8%, no return stack costs 0.35 points. Bimodal is
chosen because the extra history machinery buys under 0.2 points.

title: EX path surgery round 2: flat ALU result mux, ID-side operand pre-mux, decode-time redirect terms, narrow ID/EX flush (IPC-neutral)
motivation:
Measured on the current champion with `make timing TARGET=bench` (Gowin,
placement option 0: 84.7 MHz; scored median 75.8 MHz). The 25 worst paths
are three equal-length groups (16.9-17.1 ns arrival, ~11.5 ns data path),
all starting at MEM/WB.rd_val / MEM/WB.reg_write and sharing the 2-LUT EX
forward mux (each hop ~0.4 ns cell + ~1.0 ns route):
  A. -> alu_a mux (is_auipc) -> 32-bit adder -> SIX LUT levels of result
     muxing (alu.sv 11-way `case` on binary alu_op, then is_jump / is_muldiv
     select, then ex_busy-bubble / stall-hold / reset) -> EX/MEM.alu_result.
     4.9 ns of the 11.5 ns is spent after the adder sum.
  B. -> branch compare carry chain -> 1.4 ns route -> FOUR LUT levels of
     redirect/flush logic (branch_op select, misalign check, is_jump, then
     flush_id) -> `reset||flush` LUT with fanout 161 (0.9 ns net) -> sync
     clear of every ID/EX flop (rs1_val, rs2_val, pc, ctrl ...).
  C. -> same redirect cone -> PC register mux/enable (pc_2..pc_30).

alone gains nothing (LESSONS: a one-bottleneck fix lands at the bottom of
its range). None of this logic affects cycle counts, so every ns removed
is fitness; the acceptance bar (+4.6%) needs ~0.6 ns off all three.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Cut all three groups in one IPC-neutral change (CoreMark cycles must stay
exactly 4585414), keeping the forward mux as is:
A1. Flat ALU result select. ID pre-decodes one-hot result-class bits into
    ID/EX (sel_add, sel_logic with a 2-bit logic op, sel_shift, sel_slt,
    sel_link, sel_muldiv; LUI becomes add with a=0). alu.sv uses ONE 33-bit
    add/sub adder shared by ADD/SUB/SLT/SLTU (SLT/SLTU from sign/carry of
    the subtract) and ONE right barrel shifter (bit-reversed in/out for
    SLL, fill bit for SRA) instead of adder + subtractor + 2 comparators +
    3 shifters. The EX/MEM.alu_result D input becomes a flat AND-OR of
    {sum, logic, shift, slt, pc+4 (computed in ID, carried in ID/EX),
    md_result}: target <= 3 LUT levels after the sum instead of 6.
A2. Take hold/bubble out of the data D-mux: EX/MEM data fields
    (alu_result, mem_addr, write_data, rs*_val, pc ...) use clock-enable
    = !stall only and are NOT cleared on the ex_busy bubble or reset; only
    valid and the side-effect ctrl bits (reg_write, mem_read, mem_write,
    is_illegal, ...) keep the synchronous clear. Forwarding stays safe
    because it is already qualified by the registered reg_write.
A3. Operand pre-mux in ID: ID/EX stores op_a (pc for AUIPC, 0 for LUI,
    else rs1) and op_b (imm when alu_src, else rs2) plus separate ALU
    forward-match bits that are cleared when the operand is not a register
    read. EX then has only the 3:1 forward mux in front of the adder (one
    LUT level + ~1 ns route removed). The raw forwarded rs1/rs2 muxes stay
    for branch compare, store data, the rs1+imm address adder and muldiv.
B1. Decode-time redirect terms: pc is always 4-aligned, so target
    misalignment of JAL/branches is just imm[1] (known in ID) and for JALR
    it is addr_sum[1]. ID/EX carries jal_ok, br_ok and one-hot compare
    selects (use_eq, use_lt, use_ltu, invert). redirect = jal_ok |
    (is_jalr & ~addr_sum[1]) | (br_ok & (cond ^ inv)), with the compare
    result entering the LAST LUT: <= 2 levels after the carry chain
    instead of 4. Trap/reg_write gating semantics are unchanged.

    and the side-effect ctrl bits (reg_write, mem_read, mem_write,

title: Decoupled front-end: fall-through fetch FIFO so fetch runs ahead during back-end stalls
motivation:
Fetch and execute are rigidly coupled today: the PC only advances when the
whole pipeline advances (stall_if = load_use || imem_stall || dmem_stall ||
ex_busy) and IF/ID is purely combinational. The bench draws imem_ready and
dmem_ready independently every cycle (~22% not-ready each, regardless of
what the core requests). So every back-end stall cycle (dmem wait in MEM,
load-use bubble, second MUL cycle, 36-cycle DIV) throws away a cycle in
which the instruction bus was ready 78% of the time, and every later imem
stall inserts a bubble that a buffered instruction could have filled.

Measured on the current champion RTL (Verilator, CoreMark, --istall
--dstall, same harness and flags as the fitness eval; all runs print the
canonical CRCs and "Correct operation validated"):
  champion (coupled fetch)                    4,585,414 cycles
  + 2-entry fall-through fetch FIFO           4,394,789  (-4.16%)
  + also fetch when full && dequeuing         4,386,473  (-4.34%)
  + 4-entry FIFO                              4,383,577  (-4.40%, +4.60% iter/cycle)
CoreMark retires 2.937M instructions in the bracket, so the fetch-bound
floor is (2.937M + wrong-path fetches)/0.78 ~= 4.23M cycles: the FIFO
already recovers more than half of the gap between champion and floor,
and depth beyond 4 buys nothing.
NOT measured: Fmax of the prototype (no Gowin run fitted in the budget).
The champion's critical path is MEM/WB.rd_val -> EX forward mux -> ALU ->
EX/MEM.alu_result (17.1 ns, 15 levels), which this change does not touch.

   a small FIFO of {pc, instr} between IF and ID (prototype: shift-register

title: Timing-neutral fetch-cycle branch prediction on the 75.8 MHz core: JAL folding + bimodal PHT + RAS, verified in EX by a 1-bit direction check
motivation:
Every taken branch / JAL / JALR still costs one bubble (EX redirect kills
the instruction in ID). hyp-20261124-003-r1s2 measured this on the scored
CoreMark run: 2.94M instructions, 18.1% branches (55.6% taken), 49.6k JAL,
13.8k JALR (all but ~30 are returns) = 359k redirect bubbles, 7.96% of all
cycles (perfect-predictor ceiling +8.65% iter/cycle). Its fetch-cycle
bimodal + RAS predictor passed formal + cosim and removed 317,265 cycles
(4,491,485 -> 4,174,220, redirects 359k -> 40k, 92.5% direction accuracy,
0 return mispredicts). It only "regressed" because it was built on the

    pred_target = pc + (is_jal ? J-imm : B-imm) (own 2:1 imm mux, not

    addressed by the PC *register* (never by next_pc: a BSRAM/sync read
    would put the redirect path in front of RAM address pins - the
    inference trap from hyp-001). No global history: trace model says
    gshare adds < 0.2 points.

    on JAL/JALR with rd in {x1,x5}, pop on ret. RAS moves only on the
    consume strobe (!stall_if && !redirect, the condition under which ID/EX
    captures a valid instruction), so it never sees a wrong-path
    instruction and needs no repair.
  - never predict taken when the target has bit 1 set (a misaligned target
    traps in EX and falls through to pc+4, exactly as today).
  - next_pc = redirect ? redirect_target : stall ? pc
            : pred_taken ? pred_target : pc+4. The late EX `redirect`
    stays the outermost select: same depth for the EX path as today.
  - ID/EX carries pred_taken (1 bit), the 2-bit counter read, and for ret
    only the predicted target (RAS top) + a registered `pred_ret` bit.

is required because riscv-formal drives a symbolic instruction stream):
  - BRANCH: redirect = is_branch & (branch_cond ^ pred_taken). The XOR
    with a registered bit folds into the existing branch_taken LUT. The
    target is NOT compared: pred_target was computed from the same
    pc/instr that now sit in ID/EX, so it is right by construction.
    redirect_target = pc + (pred_taken ? 4 : imm): the existing

implementation_notes:
# hyp-20261124-003-r2s2 — fetch-cycle branch prediction (JAL fold + bimodal PHT + RAS), 1-bit EX verify

## What changed

- `rtl/branch_pred.sv` (new): pre-decode of the raw fetched instruction
  (`is_jal`, `is_branch` excluding reserved funct3 2/3, `is_ret` = JALR
  funct3==0, rs1 in {x1,x5}, rd not in {x1,x5}, imm==0), dedicated
  `pc + (instr[3] ? J-imm : B-imm)` adder, 1024x2-bit bimodal PHT
  (`syn_ramstyle="distributed_ram"`, no reset, async read by the PC
  register, sync write from EX/MEM-registered signals), 8-entry RAS that
  moves only on `consume = !stall_if && !redirect`. Never predicts a
  target whose low two bits are non-zero.
- `rtl/if_stage.sv`: instantiates `branch_pred`; next PC = reset > EX
  redirect > hold on stall > (`pred_taken ? pred_target : pc+4`). Prediction
  fields go out in the IF/ID bundle.
- `rtl/core_pkg.sv`: `pred_taken`, `pred_ret`, `pht_ctr[1:0]`,
  `ras_target[29:0]` in `if_id_t` / `id_ex_t`; `pht_ctr`, `train_valid` in
  `ex_mem_t`.
- `rtl/id_stage.sv`: latches the prediction fields into ID/EX (cleared by
  the existing flush).
- `rtl/ex_stage.sv`: `redirect` is now "mispredict":
  - BRANCH: `is_branch & !br_tgt_mis & (branch_cond ^ pred_taken)`; target
    not compared. `br_tgt_mis` is a function of registered pc/imm bits only.
  - JAL: removed from the redirect logic entirely (predicted taken iff the
    target is aligned, i.e. iff it does not trap, so the PC is always right).
  - JALR: `pred_ret ? rs1[31:1] != {ras_target,0} : !addr_sum[1]` — equality
    of the forwarded rs1 against a register, no adder in front for a
    predicted ret.
  - `redirect_target` = JALR sum, or `pc + (pred_taken ? 4 : imm)`; a
    predicted ret that traps on misaligned rs1 goes to pc+4 (select uses the
    early `rs1[1]`).
  - `pc_next` / misalign trap / `ctrl_with_trap` are untouched (architectural).
  - EX/MEM carries `pht_ctr` and `train_valid` (= valid BRANCH captured).
- `rtl/core.sv`: wires PHT training from EX/MEM (`train_valid`,
  `pc[11:2]`, `branch_taken`, `pht_ctr`) into `if_stage`.
- `test/test_branch_pred.py` (new): 7 cocotb tests (JAL always taken,
  misaligned targets never predicted, counter training/saturation, reserved
  BRANCH / near-miss JALR encodings not predicted, RAS pairing, RAS frozen
  without consume, RAS wraparound).

## Deviations from the plan

- `branch_pred` is instantiated inside `if_stage` rather than `core.sv`
  (fewer top-level wires; same logic).
- The RAS stores only target bits [31:2] and `ras_target` is 30 bits, so a
  predicted return target is 4-aligned by construction (no "bit 1 set"
  check needed on the RAS path, and uninitialised RAS contents cannot
  produce a misaligned PC).
- The fetch pre-decode also checks JALR funct3==0 and excludes BRANCH
  funct3 2/3, so `pred_taken` implies the full decoder sees a legal
  BRANCH/JAL/JALR. This is what lets EX drop JAL from the redirect and
  skip any "predicted but not a control-flow instruction" recovery term.
- The registered-mispredict fallback and the 256-entry PHT fallback were
  not needed (see timing below) and are not implemented.

## Measurements (local)

- Lint: `verilator --lint-only -Wall` clean.
- Cosim: `NRET=1 make cosim TARGET=bench` -> `passed: true`, 2 ELFs.
- CoreMark (`--bench --istall --dstall`): 4,267,527 bracketed cycles
  (champion: 4,585,414) = +7.45% iter/cycle; CRCs correct, "Correct
  operation validated." present.
- `make timing TARGET=bench` (Gowin, place option 0 only): 83.705 MHz,
  17.24 ns. Hypothesis quotes 84.7 MHz / 17.10 ns for the champion on the
  same option (I did not re-run the baseline myself). Worst paths are the
  same two families as before: MEM/WB -> forward mux -> ALU ->
  EX/MEM.alu_result (paths 1-2) and MEM/WB -> u_ex -> u_if -> ID/EX
  flush (paths 3-5, 35 cells, same cell count as the quoted baseline).
  No fetch adder / PHT / RAS path appears in the top 5.
  Area: logic 3296, registers 690, LUT-RAM 104.
- Unit test: `pytest test/test_branch_pred.py` passes.

## Concerns

- Only place option 0 was timed; the score uses the median over 3
  options, so the ~1.2% option-0 delta may or may not carry over.
- Correctness of "JAL never redirects" and "predicted-taken branch needs no
  target check" relies on the fetch-side `sum[1:0]` and the EX-side
  `branch_target[1:0]` being the same function of the same pc/instr — keep
  the two immediates in sync if either imm_gen or the pre-decode changes.
- PHT and RAS storage have no reset (hint only). Simulation starts them at
  0; the FPGA bitstream initialises them, formal treats them as arbitrary.
- Local `make formal` / `make cosim` default to the nret=2 contract and
  fail to elaborate for this nret=1 core; the correct local invocations are
  `RTL_DIR=cores/bench/rtl CORE_NAME=bench bash formal/run_all.sh` and
  `NRET=1 make cosim TARGET=bench`.
- Process note: my first two edits (core_pkg.sv, id_stage.sv) were applied
  with an inline `python3 -` heredoc rather than the edit tool. No helper
  file was written and `git status` shows only cores/bench/ paths.

## Formal status

PASS on the first RTL attempt, no fixes needed:
`RTL_DIR=cores/bench/rtl CORE_NAME=bench bash formal/run_all.sh` ->
`Formal: 53 passed, 0 failed` (nret=1: wrapper_si.sv + checks_si.cfg; all
insn checks plus pc_fwd, pc_bwd, reg, unique, liveness, causal, ill, cover).

An earlier `make formal TARGET=bench` run reported 0/105, but that was the
nret=2 wrapper failing to elaborate (`io_rvfi_valid_1 does not exist`),
not an RTL counterexample; the same applies to a first `make cosim` built
with `-DNRET=2`.

title: ID-side operand bypass: forward into the ID/EX D inputs so EX has no forward mux (IPC-neutral, every EX path starts at a flop)
motivation:
Measured on the 242.26 champion with `make timing TARGET=bench` (13 s per
run; placement option 0 = 105.1 MHz, data delay 9.48 ns, 10 levels). All
25 worst paths start at MEM/WB.rd_val (or a fwd_* select flop) and go
through the EX forward mux first:
  branch (paths 1-14, 9.48 ns): MEM/WB.rd_val -> 1.48 ns net -> 2-LUT 3:1
    forward mux (0.93 ns) -> 1.23 ns net -> compare carry chain (1.27 ns)
    -> 1.67 ns net -> 3 LUTs of PC select / kill_id -> pc_q CE/D and the
    ID/EX control clear.
  ALU loop (paths 15, 19-21, 25, 9.42 ns): MEM/WB.rd_val -> 1.18 ns net
    -> 2-LUT forward mux (1.20 ns) -> 2.15 ns net -> adder (1.86 ns) ->
    2-LUT flat result AND-OR (2.79 ns with nets) -> EX/MEM.alu_result.
So ~2.4 ns of each 9.4-9.5 ns path (25%) is "get MEM/WB.rd_val across the
die and through the forward mux" before any EX work starts. The flat ALU
select, late PC select and narrow flush were already done in r2s0; the
forward mux is the one remaining level shared by both critical families,
so cutting it moves both at once (LESSONS: a one-family fix gains nothing).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move forwarding from the head of EX to the tail of ID. id_stage already
relies on the lock-step fact: whenever ID/EX captures (no hold, no kill),
the EX instruction moves to EX/MEM and the MEM instruction to MEM/WB at
the same edge. So instead of registering fwd_* selects and muxing in EX,
the ID/EX operand registers capture the producer's value directly:
  D = m_ex  ? EX alu_result (combinational, value going into EX/MEM)
    : m_mem ? MEM rd value  (mem_to_reg ? load_data : EX/MEM.alu_result,
                             the value going into MEM/WB.rd_val)
    :         regfile read data (write-first bypass already covers WB)
with the existing m_rs*_ex / m_rs*_mem match terms (rd != 0, rd == rs,
ex_reg_write_next / mem_reg_write_next) as selects. Hold cases stay
exact: load-in-EX is the load-use kill; dmem stall and ex_busy assert
hold_id (data CE = !hold), and on the release cycle the same lock-step
rule applies (M-op result is on alu_result when md_done).
EX then reads rs1_val / rs2_val / op_b straight from ID/EX flops: no
forward mux in front of the branch compare, the ALU adder, the rs1+imm
address adder (BSRAM address / JALR target) or the store data.
Details:
1. Operand registers: rs1_val, rs2_val (raw, bypassed) and op_b
   (alu_src ? imm : bypassed rs2). Drop op_a: fold LUI / AUIPC into the
   pre-gated `link` value in ID (LUI: imm, AUIPC: the existing pc+imm
   adder output, JAL/JALR: pc+4, else 0) with sel_add = 0 for them, so
   ALU operand a == rs1_val. Remove all eight fwd_* flops.
2. Build each D input as a flat one-hot AND-OR with the two late values
   (EX alu_result, load_data) on the LAST LUT5 and the early values
   (EX/MEM.alu_result register, regfile data) pre-combined:
     D = sel_ex & alu_result | sel_ld & load_data | early
   so the ALU loop is flop -> adder -> result AND-OR -> one bypass level
   -> flop (the 2-LUT mux + 1.2-1.5 ns source net at the head is replaced
   by one level at the tail), and the dmem path is BSRAM -> load align ->
   one bypass level -> ID/EX.
3. MEM/WB no longer feeds EX: remove fwd_mem_wb / the hold_wb data
   retention requirement (keep valid clear on dmem stall); MEM/WB.rd_val
   fans out only to the regfile.
4. muldiv: operands are stable ID/EX flops for the whole M-op, so drop
   the a_q / b_q latches (a_lat / b_lat = ID/EX rs*_val) and, to keep the
   DSP out of the new alu_result -> ID/EX path, spend the first EX cycle
   on the multiply itself: prod_q <= $signed(a33) * $signed(b33) in
   S_IDLE, hi/lo select from the product register in S_MUL. MUL stays
   exactly 2 EX cycles; ALTOPS branch keeps the same 2-cycle handshake.
Cycle count must stay exactly 4585414 (pure timing change; formal reg /
insn checks prove the bypass). Estimate from the measured path pieces:
branch family 9.48 -> ~7.1 ns, ALU loop 9.42 -> ~8.0-8.6 ns, i.e. option-0
Fmax 105 -> ~115-122 MHz. Implementer: re-run `make timing` after the
change; if the load_data -> ID/EX path or the alu_result fanout (now 4
loads per bit) becomes the worst path, keep the late term on the final
LUT / duplicate nothing, and as a fallback leave ONLY mem_to_reg

title: Decoupled, self-steering front-end on the 111 MHz core: fall-through fetch FIFO + fetch-cycle JAL / backward-branch following, verified by registered ID/EX bits only
motivation:
The core is fetch-bound, not execute-bound. Scored CoreMark run: 2.94M
instructions in 4,585,414 cycles (CPI 1.56) although the back end only needs
~3.5M cycles (instructions + MUL + load-use + dmem waits). The bench draws
imem_ready and dmem_ready independently (~22% not-ready each), so at most 0.78
instructions/cycle can be fetched; today the PC also holds during every
back-end hold (dmem stall, load-use, ex_busy), and 359k taken transfers
(296k branches, 49.6k JAL, 13.8k JALR) each kill a fetched instruction.

Both halves were measured separately on IPC-identical cores, and both lost
only to a same-round Fmax sibling:
  - r2s1 fetch FIFO + JAL following: 4,585,414 -> 4,319,449 cycles (+6.16%)
  - r2s2 fetch-cycle prediction:     4,585,414 -> 4,267,527 cycles (+7.45%)
They are super-additive: once the FIFO makes the core fetch-bound, every
wrong-path fetch costs 1/0.78 cycles instead of 1. The FIFO-only run used
~3.37M ready fetch slots for 2.94M instructions + ~310k squashed fetches.
Following backward branches statically (r1s2 trace model: static
backward-taken = +5.8% vs +7.6% for a bimodal PHT) cuts EX redirects from
~310k to ~127k, so fetch demand drops to ~3.07M slots -> ~4.05-4.12M cycles,
i.e. +11..13% iter/cycle, with no predictor table at all.

Timing measured now on the champion (`make timing TARGET=bench`, option 0,
105.1 MHz): the 25 worst paths are three co-critical EX families within
0.1 ns of each other (data path 9.38-9.48 ns), all behind the EX forward mux:
  MEM/WB.rd_val -> compare -> pc_q[*]                       9.48 ns
  MEM/WB.rd_val -> compare -> kill -> ID/EX ctrl flops      9.43 ns
  MEM/WB.rd_val / fwd_a_mem -> adder -> EX/MEM.alu_result   9.42 ns
So Fmax is balanced across three loops (no single structural cut pays), and
no fetch/decode path is in the top 25. In the timed netlist imem_data is a
flop (LFSR) and imem_addr only feeds an XOR, so the fetch cycle starts at a
register. The gain must come from IPC, and the front-end must add nothing
to those three families.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace if_stage with a decoupled fetch unit (single structural change):

1. Fetch PC `fpc_q` advances on `fire = imem_ready && !full` (registered
   count only), independent of back-end holds. A 4-entry fall-through FIFO of
   {pc[31:2], instr, followed} sits between imem and ID: ID sees the head, or
   imem_data directly when count==0 (one flop-selected 2:1 mux; prefer a
   shift FIFO so the head is always slot 0 and there is no read mux).
   hazard_unit: avail = count!=0 || imem_ready; kill_id = load_use || !avail
   || redirect; deq = avail && !load_use && !hold_id; stall_if disappears.
2. Self-steering in the fetch cycle, from the fetched word only (no tables):
   follow = fire && ((JAL && !immJ[1]) || (BRANCH && instr[31] && !immB[1]));
   next fpc = follow ? fpc + (instr[3] ? immJ : immB) : fpc+4. One 30-bit
   adder whose immediate format select is instr[3] (a flop); the direction
   "prediction" is instr[31] (a flop). `followed` travels with the entry.
3. EX verify with ZERO added EX logic: fold `followed` into the ID-registered
   redirect terms. JAL never redirects in EX (aligned -> followed, misaligned
   -> already traps in ID). Followed branch: redir_c1 = br_inv, redir_c0 =
   !br_inv (redirect iff NOT taken) with redirect target pc+4; non-followed
   branch unchanged. redirect = jalr_go | (br_cond ? redir_c1 : redir_c0)
   stays byte-identical, and the pc mux keeps its late-select shape
   (nxt_c1/nxt_c0 built from early signals: redir_cX ? alt_target : fseq).
   The alternate target must not add a level behind the pc+imm adder in ID
   (mux the immediate to 4, or carry pc+4 in a separate ID/EX register and
   select with the registered `followed` bit in parallel with the fetch adder).
   br_bad / jalr_bad trap behaviour unchanged (misaligned targets are never
   followed). RVFI pc_next = redirect ? target : predicted-next (RVFI-only
   logic, pruned from the timed netlist).
4. The late `redirect` gets exactly one new sink: synchronous clear of the
   FIFO count (3 flops). It must never reach FIFO entry muxes or enables.

Expected: ~4.05-4.12M cycles (+11..13% iter/cycle) at unchanged Fmax
(+~250 LUT4 / +300 FF). Break-even is a 10% Fmax loss. Risks to time before
trusting the cycle count: (a) fetch chain LFSR/fpc flop -> adder -> fseq ->
nxt_c -> pc mux (est. ~7 ns, limit 9.4); (b) the head/bypass mux adds one
level in front of decoder / regfile read / load-use compare in ID. Fallbacks
in order: 2-entry FIFO; drop branch following and keep FIFO + JAL (+6.2%).
A bimodal PHT / RAS (another ~2 points) is deliberately left out: its
1024-entry async read is the timing risk the r2s2 lesson flagged at 9 ns.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Port the predictor to the r2s0 core, conditional branches + JAL only.
No RAS / JALR prediction: it is worth ~0.35 points and would put a 30-bit
equality on jalr_go, the outermost pc_q select. JALR stays exactly as is.

FETCH (if_stage, all from imem_data flops / pc_q flops):
- pre-decode: f_jal = opcode==1101111; f_br = opcode==1100011 && funct3 not
  2/3 (so pred_taken implies the full decoder sees a legal JAL / BRANCH);
  f_al = !(instr[3] ? instr[21] : instr[8])  (target bit 1 clear; a
  misaligned target is never predicted, so the trap fall-through pc+4 is
  where the PC already went).
- target: ptgt[31:2] = pc_q + imm[31:2], imm = instr[3] ? J-imm : B-imm.
  Only imm bits 1-4, 11 and 12-19 differ between B and J (13 LUT3s);
  bits 5-10 and the sign bits go straight into the carry chain.
- direction: 2-bit bimodal PHT, 512 x 2, syn_ramstyle="distributed_ram",
  no reset, async read at pc_q[10:2] (parallel to the imem access; 32:1
  read mux fits LUT + MUX2_LUT5..8, one routed level after the RAM16).
- pred_take = f_al & (f_jal | f_br & pht[1]);
  seq = stall ? pc_q : pred_take ? ptgt : pc_inc.  The late select
  (jalr_go ? jalr_sum : br_cond ? nxt_c1 : nxt_c0) is untouched. A
  prediction is acted on exactly in the cycle ID/EX captures the
  instruction (not captured => stall_if or redirect => seq is not used),
  so the registered pred_taken always matches where the PC went and no
  repair / wrong-path state exists.

VERIFY (id_stage flops only, ex_stage redirect logic unchanged):
  br_ok     = dec_is_branch & !imm[1]
  redir_c1 <= br_ok & (!instr[12] ^ pred_taken)   // JAL term removed
  redir_c0 <= br_ok & ( instr[12] ^ pred_taken)
  btarget  <= pred_taken ? pc4 : ptgt             // the ALTERNATE path
redirect therefore means "compare disagrees with the prediction" and goes
to the other path, with no target compare (fetch and ID use the same
adder output) and no extra LUT behind br_cond. Reusing ptgt for btarget
also deletes id_stage's own pc+imm adder (it sat behind imm_gen).
br_bad / jal_bad / jalr_bad trap logic is untouched (architectural).

TRAIN: the PHT index is pc[10:2] (already in ID/EX and EX/MEM); ID/EX
carries the 2-bit counter read;
EX/MEM registers {is valid branch, taken = br_cond ^ br_inv, counter};
the saturating update is written from those EX/MEM flops the cycle after
resolve (idempotent under dmem-stall holds). Nothing fans out of the
compare except one extra flop D pin.

RVFI (untimed, pruned by synthesis): keep the architectural taken terms
(old redir_c1/c0 meaning) and pc+imm in ID/EX as RVFI-only fields so
pc_next = jalr_go ? jalr target : taken ? pc+imm : pc+4.

Expected: cycles 4,585,414 -> ~4.28M (+7.1% iter/cycle: r2s2's measured
+7.45% minus the ret part), +~150 LUT4, +16 LUT-RAM, Fmax unchanged
(same critical path, same 10 levels) -> ~259, vs the 253.4 acceptance bar.
Break-even is a 6.6% Fmax loss; acceptance needs < 2.3% loss.

untouched champion first and compare the SAME placement option afterwards
(judge by cycles + same-option diff, not the scored median). The top paths
must still be MEM/WB.rd_val -> u_ex -> u_if.pc_q. If a path starting at
imem_data/LFSR or pc_q -> PHT appears in the top 5, apply in order:
(a) 256-entry PHT, (b) two parallel adders (pc+B-imm, pc+J-imm) selected
by instr[3] after the carry chains, (c) PHT-free static prediction
pred_take = f_al & (f_jal | f_br & instr[31]) (modelled +5.8%).
Never trade Fmax for the predictor. Local commands (nret=1):
`NRET=1 make cosim TARGET=bench`,
`RTL_DIR=cores/bench/rtl CORE_NAME=bench bash formal/run_all.sh`.

title: Post-compare depth surgery: CE-free PC register with a true one-LUT late select, gated compare chains, one-LUT kill and ALU result merge (IPC-neutral)
motivation:
Measured on the 242.26 champion with `make timing TARGET=bench` (Gowin,
placement option 0, 105.1 MHz, 9.48 ns data path, 10 levels). The worst 5
paths all end at the CLOCK ENABLE of the PC flops (cpu/u_if/pc_q_*_s1/CE),
not at D. Breakdown of path 1 (MEM/WB.rd_val_11 -> pc_q_2/CE):
  1.48 net + 0.93 (LUT5 forward mux) + 1.23 net + 1.27 (compare carry chain)
  then AFTER the carry chain: 1.67 net -> LUT nxt_c0_29_s9 (0.37) -> 0.17
  -> LUT nxt_c0_29_s5 (0.37, fanout 39) -> 0.70 net -> LUT pc_q_28_s3
  (0.33, fanout 30) -> 0.73 net -> CE.  = 4.33 ns of 9.48 ns.

netlist: Gowin saw D==Q under `stall` behind the late select, extracted a
clock enable = f(jalr_go, br_cond, redir_c*, stall) and put THREE LUT
levels plus two high-fanout nets behind the compare (r3s2 saw the same
merge and needed syn_keep on nxt_c1/nxt_c0). r3s0 removed the whole EX
forward mux and Fmax did not move (111.16 vs 111.09) with the critical

not the head of EX, is what pins the clock. Fetch-side IPC ideas keep
losing because they add sinks to exactly this tail; shortening it is
IPC-neutral and also makes room for them later.

title: Retime the redirect across the PC register (flush_q + fetch-address select, same 1-bubble penalty) so a predicted, buffered front end hangs off flops only
motivation:
Three front-end changes delivered exactly their modelled iter/cycle (fetch
FIFO +6.2%, fetch-cycle predictor +7.1..7.5%, both together +12.8%:
4,585,414 -> 4,063,788 CoreMark cycles) and all lost on Fmax for one
structural reason: every one of them hung more endpoints / fanout / area
behind the late EX net `redirect` (r3s1: 111.1 -> 94.0 MHz, all five worst
paths forward mux -> compare -> redirect -> fetch-unit state; r3s2: -> 105.9).
A fresh Gowin run on the champion (placement option 0, 105.1 MHz) shows why
there is no room: MEM/WB.rd_val -> fwd mux -> compare -> redirect -> pc_q/CE
is 9.479 ns, -> kill_id -> ID/EX control flops 9.428 ns, and the ALU loop
rd_val -> fwd mux -> adder -> EX/MEM.alu_result 9.417 ns. The redirect has
~40 sinks two mux levels deep and sits 0.06 ns above a loop that cannot be
cut, so anything added behind it sets Fmax. The fix is topological, not
another micro-cut: the late compare result does not need to reach the PC in
the resolve cycle to keep a 1-bubble penalty.

title: Ahead-pipelined next-line BTB: PC steered only by flops, verified by early pc_q==correct-npc compares
motivation:
Every taken branch / JAL costs one bubble (EX redirect kills the ID slot): 359k bubbles =
7.96% of CoreMark cycles, perfect-predictor ceiling +8.65% iter/cycle. Two predictor ports
already proved the IPC (+7.45% r2s2, +7.09% r3s2: 4,585,414 -> 4,281,978 cycles, formal
first try) but both steered the PC from the *fetched word in the same cycle*:
imem_data -> pre-decode / imm select -> 30-bit pc+imm adder -> seq -> nxt_c -> pc_q.
On the 111 MHz champion that chain is co-critical with the EX loop (14.619 vs 14.632 ns),
the scored median fell 111.1 -> 105.9 MHz and the result (247.4) missed the 253.4 bar.
The lesson is not "prediction does not pay" but "no decode, adder or RAM read may sit
between a flop and pc_q in the fetch cycle". This hypothesis is a different predictor

title: Zero-stall MUL fast path: preload the multiplier operand regs at the ID/EX edge, stall only when an operand needs forwarding
motivation:
Every MUL on the 117.5 MHz champion pays a fixed +1 EX cycle: cycle 1
only latches the post-forward operands into muldiv's a_q/b_q (ex_busy),
cycle 2 runs a_q/b_q -> DSP -> ALU `other` -> EX/MEM. The sequential
M unit cost 93,929 CoreMark cycles when it was introduced
(4,491,485 -> 4,585,414), i.e. ~94k visible MUL stall cycles = 2.2% of
today's 4,281,466.
That latch cycle is only needed when an operand must be forwarded. In
the CoreMark -O3 binary (disassembled for this proposal) GCC schedules
the hot matrix_test loops as `lh; lh; addi; addi; mul`, so the MUL
operands were produced >= 3 instructions earlier and arrive through the
regfile (WB write-first bypass) with all four fwd_rs* bits 0:
mul_const @1730, mul_vect @1814, mul_matrix @1910 and the first
bitextract mul @1a24 need no forwarding; only the second bitextract mul
@1a3c (`andi; andi; mul`) does. With N=9 that is (2*729+162)/2349 = 69%
of the dynamic MULs (static estimate, not a simulated count).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Keep the 2-cycle reg -> DSP -> EX/MEM multiply exactly as it is, but
load its operand registers one cycle earlier in the common case:

1. muldiv a_q/b_q (33 bit) get a second load leg: whenever ID/EX
   captures (`!hold_id`, same CE as the ID/EX data group) they take
   the regfile read data rs1_data/rs2_data with the sign bit chosen
   from the raw instr[14:12] of the instruction in ID. So when an M-op
   reaches EX with no forward bit set, a_q/b_q already hold its exact
   operands (== ID/EX.rs1_val/rs2_val).
2. need_fix = fwd_rs1_ex | fwd_rs1_mem | fwd_rs2_ex | fwd_rs2_mem
   (ID/EX flops only). MUL* with !need_fix: `done` is asserted in the
   first EX cycle (state stays S_IDLE), result = mul_res, ex_busy = 0.
   The product lands in EX/MEM.alu_result like any ALU result, so the
   next instruction forwards it with NO stall and no new hazard term.
3. need_fix = 1 (and all DIV/REM): today's behaviour unchanged - the
   first EX cycle (ex_busy, ID/EX held) overwrites a_q/b_q with the
   post-forward rs1/rs2 (`patch = start && need_fix && state==S_IDLE`,
   flops only; patch implies hold_id so the two load legs are mutually
   exclusive: D = patch ? fwd : regfile, CE = !hold_id | patch), then
   S_MUL / S_INIT as now. Default the result mux to mul_res

and a_q/b_q hold, done stays 1, and no forward source is in use.

handshake.

EX cycle (a_q/b_q -> DSP -> hi/lo -> other -> alu out). New logic:

path (imem_data -> LUT-RAM -> written/bypass mux -> flop, well short

the existing state decode). Nothing is added to the ALU loop

title: Decoupled fetch via pointer-only circular LUT-RAM buffer: PC advance and entry writes depend on imem_ready/flops only
motivation:
The bench draws imem_ready and dmem_ready independently (~22% not-ready each), so
fetch throughput (0.78 instr/cycle) is the IPC ceiling and every backend stall
(dmem stall with a LOAD/STORE in MEM, load-use, ex_busy for MUL/DIV) also throws
away a fetch slot that was ready. A fall-through fetch buffer reclaims those slots:
r4s1 measured 4,281,466 -> 4,020,117 CoreMark cycles (+6.5% iter/cycle, formal
53/53) with a 2-entry shift FIFO on exactly this core, but reverted it at 89.5 MHz
because of two fetch-internal chains at 11.1 ns: (a) imem_data -> head mux ->
load-use compare -> pop -> shift/enable of 95 entry flops, and (b) flush_q -> fa ->
PHT read -> pred -> alternate select -> head mux -> ID/EX btarget. Both are
artefacts of the shift-FIFO topology, not of decoupling. This is the only IPC item
left that is larger than the 4.6% acceptance margin (better predictors model at
<0.5 points; the champion's worst path is the untouched EX ALU loop, 9 cells), so
it deserves one topologically different attempt. In the timed netlist
(fpga/core_bench_si.sv) io_imemData, io_imemReady and io_dmemReady are all plain
flops, so anything gated only by them and by core flops is an early signal.

title: Predictor in its own fetch stage: prediction-directed prefetch into a registered LUT-RAM instruction queue (no fall-through)
motivation:
Direction/target accuracy is nearly exhausted on this core. The trace model
put the perfect-predictor ceiling at 359k one-cycle redirect bubbles of the
4,585,414-cycle run (+8.65% iter/cycle); the shipped aligned-JAL follow +
512x2 bimodal PHT already runs 4,281,466 cycles (+7.1%), so only ~55k
bubbles (~1.3%) are left for RAS / gshare / BTB work - a pure accuracy
upgrade cannot clear the 4.6% acceptance margin (r4s2's ahead-pipelined BTB
landed at 4,291,901 cycles, i.e. no IPC over the champion).

What the predictor can still buy is fetch slots. Today the prediction is
only used in cycles where ID consumes: every back-end stall cycle (dmem
stall on ~22% of memory ops, load-use, M-op busy) discards the fetch even
when imem was ready, and the instruction must win the 78% imem draw again.
Two measured ports show what following the predicted path through those
cycles is worth: 4,063,788 cycles (r3s1) and 4,020,117 cycles (r4s1's
reverted 2-entry FIFO), i.e. about +6.5% iter/cycle on top of the champion.
Both lost 15-20% Fmax, and both for the same structural reason: they were
FALL-THROUGH buffers, so the fetch-cycle prediction chain was concatenated
with the ID chain (flush_q -> fa -> PHT -> pred -> alternate select -> head
mux -> ID/EX btarget/link, 11.1 ns) and the consume strobe fanned into the
entry shift muxes (imem_data -> head mux -> load-use compare -> pop -> 95
entry flops, 11.1 ns). The champion itself still has the first chain
(flush_pc_q -> fa -> adder/PHT -> btarget / pc_q) within 0.02 ns of the ALU
loop, so the front end has no slack for a bypass mux.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Give the predictor its own pipeline stage and never bypass it. The fetch
engine (fa mux, PHT read, raw pre-decode, fa+B-imm / fa+J-imm adders, pc_q)
stays exactly as it is, but its output is written into a small instruction
queue and ID reads only the queue head. Nothing fetched reaches ID in the
fetch cycle, so the fetch chain ends at queue storage + pc_q and the ID
chain starts at flops/LUT-RAM outputs: the two failing chains of the FIFO
ports cannot form.

Structure:
1. Queue payload in distributed RAM (4 entries, syn_ramstyle
   "distributed_ram", never reset): {pc[31:2], instr, pred_taken, pht[1:0]}
   written at wr_ptr with write enable `accept = imem_ready & !full_q`
   (full_q / count / wr_ptr / rd_ptr are flops; full is computed from the
   registered count only, never from this cycle's pop). Async read by the
   rd_ptr flops gives the head. pc4 and the taken target are recomputed in
   ID from the head's pc/instr with two small adders (ID has slack; they
   start at RAM outputs), keeping link (pc4) separate from the
   PHT-dependent alternate as r4s1's notes require. If that ID adder turns
   out slower than storing `tgt`, store tgt[31:2] in the RAM instead.
2. Fetch steering is unchanged in content but its enable changes from "ID
   consumed" to `accept`: pc_q <= accept ? (pred_taken ? tgt : fa_inc) : fa.
   The predictor therefore keeps walking the predicted path while the back
   end is stalled, which is where the IPC comes from.
3. Consume side: head_valid = (count_q != 0) (flop-only). hazard_unit's
   kill_id = load_use | !head_valid, hold_id unchanged, pop = !hold_id &
   !load_use & head_valid moves only rd_ptr/count. Load-use compare, the
   decoder, imm_gen and the regfile read addresses take the head word.
   imem_ready no longer reaches ID/EX control at all.
4. Redirect: flush_q (already a flop) resets wr_ptr/rd_ptr/count to empty
   and selects fa = flush_pc_q as today; EX squashes the wrong-path
   instruction in ID/EX exactly as now. The head that ID would capture in
   the flush cycle is also wrong-path: gate with kill_id |= flush_q.
   PHT training, redir_c1/redir_c0, btarget/npc_pred, bp_idx stay as they
   are (pred_taken and pht now come from the queue entry).

  carries one entry as the pipeline stage and 3 as buffer, so it should
  match or beat the 2-entry fall-through FIFO's 4,020,117 cycles before the
  penalty: estimate 4.06-4.10M cycles, +4.4% to +5.5% iter/cycle.

more than ~4.11M cycles, the fallback is a flop-selected empty-queue bypass
for the redirect target only, and it must be timed on all three placement
options before it is kept.

title: Early load in EX: ID-computed dmem address register, load data forwarded like an ALU result (kills load-use + most load dmem waits)
motivation:
Cycle accounting on the champion (4,281,466 cycles, 2,922,016 retired
instructions, imem ready 100/128): fetch-attempt cycles = N/0.78125 = 3.74M
plus ~56k redirect slots, so ~485k cycles (11.3%) are pure back-end HOLD
cycles in which the PC is frozen: ~94k MUL second cycles, and ~390k of
load-use bubbles + dmem waits (0.28 expected wait per LOAD/STORE in MEM).
Four fetch-FIFO builds tried to OVERLAP these holds with imem stalls and
each paid the ~6% IPC back in Fmax (head mux in front of decode). Nobody has
tried to REMOVE the holds at their source, which needs no front-end change
at all: the three co-critical families (ALU loop, flush_q -> fa -> pc_q,
rd_val -> compare -> flush_q) are untouched.
Both load costs come from the topology "address in EX, access in MEM": the
load result exists only after MEM (load-use bubble) and the access gets
exactly one try per cycle starting in MEM. A load whose base register needs
no forwarding (r5s0 measured 69% of MUL operands are forward-free; loop
pointers / sp-relative loads are the same pattern) can have its address
ready one stage earlier.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Restructure the load path so a LOAD can complete in EX.
1. ONE dmem address register A drives io_dmemAddr (must stay a plain flop:
   the bench dmem is an async-read array that Gowin maps to BSRAM by
   absorbing this register - never put a combinational mux on io_dmemAddr).
   A.D = sel_ex ? addr_sum : id_addr, CE = !stall_ex_mem, where
   id_addr = rs1_data + sext(instr[31:20]) is a new ID-stage adder on the
   regfile read data (raw I-imm, no imm_gen mux) and
   sel_ex = (ID/EX.mem_read | ID/EX.mem_write) & !early_done (flops +
   dmem_ready only).
2. ID registers early_cand (control group, cleared on kill/reset) =
   dec_mem_read & !m_rs1_ex & !m_rs1_mem & aligned(rs1_data[1:0]+imm[1:0],
   width) & !sel_ex, plus the 2 low address bits. By construction the port
   is free next cycle (the instruction entering MEM is not a mem op).
3. EX: early_go = early_cand & !flush_q drives io_dmemREn; early_done =
   early_go & dmem_ready. The extracted/sign-extended load data, gated by
   early_done, enters the ALU AND-OR through `other`, so EX/MEM.alu_result
   holds the load value; EX/MEM.mem_read and mem_to_reg are cleared, so MEM
   does no access and can never dmem-stall for it. If dmem_ready = 0 the
   load simply continues to MEM as today (A <= addr_sum), i.e. it gets a
   free second try.
4. hazard_unit: load_use_hazard &= !early_done. The consumer then uses the
   existing fwd_*_ex path - no new forwarding source, no new mux in the ALU
   loop. RVFI mem_addr/rmask/rdata of an early load travel in RVFI-only
   EX/MEM fields (pruned by synthesis).
Memory order is safe: an early read only happens when MEM holds no mem op,
so every older store has already been accepted; the instruction in EX with
!flush_q is never wrong-path, and REn is gated by flops so no OOB read.
Expected: early candidates ~55-70% of ~650k loads; each saves 0.22 dmem-wait
cycles and 78% of its load-use bubbles -> ~150-190k cycles (+3.6..4.7%
iter/cycle). Stack the measured r5s0 rider (regfile-preloaded 1-cycle MUL
when no fwd bit is set: -65,037 cycles, +1.54%) in the same change, since
neither clears the 4.6% bar alone: total ~4.03-4.07M cycles, +5..6.5%.
Timing risks to measure on all three placement options against a
same-session baseline: (a) LFSR -> regfile read -> 13-bit add -> A mux ->
BSRAM address setup (only bits 12:2 reach the RAM); (b) BSRAM clk-to-out
2.26 ns -> load extract -> `other` -> EX/MEM.alu_result, which shares the OR
leg with the co-critical DSP product. Do NOT fix (b) with a separate
EX/MEM load field (that adds a forward source inside the ALU loop); the
fallbacks are: early path for LW only (no extract mux), or drop the MUL
rider. sel_ex should also be gated by !flush_q so the instruction fetched

title: Return prediction with zero new EX logic: flop RAS top followed in fetch, verified by the existing rs1==rs2 compare via redir_c0
motivation:
Honest sizing first. After r4s1 the only redirects left are mispredicted
conditional branches and EVERY JALR (never predicted today, one flush_q
bubble each). Trace model: 359k redirect bubbles at the old baseline, the
shipped JAL-follow + 512x2 bimodal PHT removed 304k (4,585,414 -> 4,281,466
cycles), so ~55k bubbles (~1.3% of cycles) is the whole remaining predictor
ceiling. gshare was modelled at <0.2 points; function returns were MEASURED
at ~0.35 points (r2s2 with RAS 4,267,527 cycles vs r3s2 without 4,281,978,
~14k cycles). Returns are therefore the only remaining predictor item with a
measured payoff, and they are the one JALR class a tiny structure predicts
almost perfectly.

Both earlier predictor restructures that tried to buy more than accuracy
lost: r4s2 (ahead-pipelined BTB) fell to 109.5 MHz with no cycle gain, r5s2
(predictor stage + instruction queue) timed out formal. So this slot takes
the remaining accuracy item in the cheapest possible form: no table, no new
comparator, no new late net, no change to the flush_q topology that made
r4s1 the first front-end change to gain Fmax. On its own it cannot clear the
4.6% bar (about +0.35% iter/cycle); it is sized as a near-free predictor
increment, with the already-proven r5s0 MUL preload (+1.54% measured, formal
first try) named as a separable rider per LESSONS so the slot is not spent
on a sub-margin item alone.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
A. Return-address stack, flops only (if_stage).
   - 4 entries x 30 bit + 2-bit sp, plus an explicit registered copy of the
     top entry `ras_top_q` so no sp-indexed mux sits in front of pc_q.
     Reset to 0 (pure hint; a wrong value is only a performance event).
   - Raw pre-decode from imem_data, in parallel with op_jal / op_br:
       op_ret  = (imem_data == 32'h00008067)            // jalr x0, 0(x1)
       op_call = (JAL or JALR-funct3-000 opcode) && imem_data[11:7] == 5'd1
     op_ret guarantees imm == 0, rd == x0, rs2 field == x0.
   - Follow in the fetch cycle: pred_taken |= op_ret, and the target select
     becomes tgt = op_ret ? ras_top_q : op_jal ? tgt_j : tgt_b. This is a
     flop leg selected AFTER the two fa+imm adders (r4s1 lesson: flop-
     selected mux after arithmetic, never in front), so the adder/PHT chain
     gains no level; op_ret (32-bit constant match, ~3 LUT levels) is
     shallower than the 30-bit carry chains it selects behind.
   - Update on the ID/EX capture strobe (!hold_id && !kill_id): push fa_inc
     on op_call, pop on op_ret. With the retimed redirect the instruction
     captured while a mispredicting branch sits in EX is wrong-path, so keep
     a 1-deep undo: sp_prev / top_prev registered at each update and
     restored when flush_q is set (flush_q is a flop; a wrong-path push only
     overwrote the dead slot above the top). No late EX net enters if_stage.
B. Verify with logic EX already has (id_stage / ex_stage).
   - ID: for a predicted ret, ID/EX.rs2_val <= {ras_top, 2'b00} instead of
     the regfile read (rs2 field is x0, so no forward bit can be set), and
     redir_c1 <= 0, redir_c0 <= 1. JALR has funct3 000, so br_use_eq = 1 and
     br_inv = 0 already: br_cond = cmp_eq = (ra == predicted target) and
     `br_cond ? redir_c1 : redir_c0` redirects exactly on a wrong return
     address. No new comparator, no new term behind the compare.
   - New ID/EX control bit jalr_np = JALR && !pred_ret drives jalr_go;

     pc+4 for a followed ret (pred_taken path), so a mispredicted ret whose
     ra is misaligned traps and redirects back to pc+4: make the registered
     target select `is_jalr && !addr_sum[1]` (bit 1 of a 2-bit add, early).

title: Fmax micro-opt on all three co-critical families: MEM->ID capture bypass (2:1 flop-selected EX forward muxes) + pc_q-indexed PHT with no steering in the flush cycle
motivation:
LESSONS close the IPC side for micro-opts: stall / predictor items sum to
<= 3.5% iter/cycle and every ~6% IPC build was billed ~6% Fmax. The only
micro_opt that can clear the 4.6% bar is an Fmax gain at ~zero IPC cost.
The champion (117.5 MHz, 8.5 ns) is pinned by three families within
~0.02 ns of each other:
  A. MEM/WB.rd_val -> forward mux -> ALU -> EX/MEM.alu_result (logged
     worst path: rd_val[23] -> alu_result[6], 9 cells = the shifter leg);
  B. MEM/WB.rd_val -> forward mux -> compare -> flush_q;
  C. flush_q / flush_pc_q -> fa mux -> 512-entry PHT LUT-RAM read ->
     pred_taken -> pc_q / ID/EX btarget (11 cells).
r3s0's measured path anatomy (log.jsonl) says the 3:1 forward mux is TWO
LUTs (0.93-1.20 ns) fed by a 1.2-1.5 ns cross-die net from MEM/WB.rd_val:
~25% of families A and B is spent before any EX work starts. r3s0 tried
to delete the mux completely by also putting the late EX alu_result on
the ID/EX D inputs; it netted +0.07% because (i) the then-critical
compare -> redirect -> pc_q/kill loop (38 cells) still existed - r4s1 has
since retimed it away - and (ii) it added a tail mux + 4x fanout on the
late ALU result. This hypothesis takes only the half that is free.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
(1) MEM->ID capture bypass (families A, B, address adder, store data).
When ID/EX captures, the producer two ahead sits in EX/MEM and moves to
MEM/WB at the same edge, so its value is exactly the MEM/WB.rd_val D
input. ID writes it straight into rs1_val / rs2_val / op_a / op_b using
the existing m_rs*_mem match terms, built so nothing late gets deeper:
  D = sel_ld ? load_data : early
  early = one-hot AND-OR of {EX/MEM.alu_result flop (m_mem & !mem_to_reg),
          regfile data incl. write-first bypass, pc / 0 / imm premux}
  sel_ld = m_rs*_mem & EX/MEM.ctrl.mem_to_reg (flop + raw-instr compare)
load_data sits on the LAST LUT only, so BSRAM -> extract -> 1 LUT -> flop
has the same depth as today's non-critical path into MEM/WB.rd_val (one
level shallower than r6s1's extract -> `other` -> AND-OR leg that failed).
No arithmetic is added behind the regfile read. EX then needs only
  x = fwd_*_ex ? EX/MEM.alu_result : ID/EX value
a 2:1 mux with a single flop select (1 LUT instead of 2, source flop is
the loop's own destination register, select fanout halved). The four
fwd_*_mem flops, the fwd_mem_wb port and the MEM/WB hold-for-forwarding
requirement disappear; MEM/WB.rd_val feeds only the regfile. Hold cases
stay exact because the value now lives in ID/EX (CE = !hold); muldiv
latches as before. Cycle count must stay identical apart from item 2.

pht_rd = pht[pc_q[8:0]], and do not steer in the flush cycle: gate the

op_* & !flush_q; the PHT bit stays the last AND). The fa mux and its
fanout leave the PHT read path (one level + the highest-fanout net of
family C). An aligned JAL fetched in a flush cycle is not followed and
redirects from EX through the existing mux: redir_c1 = redir_c0 =

title: Two-stage fetch around a core-internal BSRAM instruction store: hits never see the imem bus stall, bus used only for refill
motivation:
The bench draws imem_ready ~78% per cycle, so every instruction delivery
needs a ready cycle: cycles ~= (N + wrong-path fetches)/0.78 + blocked
cycles. From the logged numbers (4,281,466 cycles now, 4,020,117 with a
fetch FIFO, which is the bus-limited floor (N+R)/0.78) N+R is ~3.14M, so
~0.88M of today's cycles (~20%) are imem stall cycles. Four fetch buffers
only recovered the overlap with other stalls (+6%) and each paid ~6% Fmax;
every other remaining IPC item sums to <= 3.5%. The only large lever left
is to stop asking the bus for instructions the core has already fetched.
ARCHITECTURE.md allows logic that "hides stalls" as long as it is in the
timed netlist. CoreMark's hot code is a few KB, the FPGA has ~42 unused
BSRAMs, and no log entry has tried an instruction store. (Also checked:
the ID-side operand bypass was already built as hyp-20261124-001-r3s0 and
was a wash at 111.16 vs 111.09 MHz, so it is not re-proposed.)

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a direct-mapped instruction store (2048 entries, index pc[12:2], word =
{valid, tag pc[31:13], instr}; ~7 BSRAM, `initial` zero so valid=0 at
power-up) and make fetch two stages so no ID path starts at a BSRAM
clk-to-out:
  F  : BSRAM array read of pc_f (address pins = next fetch address).
  ID : instr comes from the BSRAM OUTPUT REGISTER (it is the IF/ID
       register; no bus/cache mux in front of decoder / regfile /
       pre-decode), pc_d flop beside it. Everything in ID/EX/MEM/WB stays.
Hit check is done in ID from flops in parallel with decode:
miss_d = !(valid & tag == pc_d[31:13]) is one more kill_id term. Misses are
rare (each hot instruction misses once), so the miss path is deliberately
slow and simple: a small FSM squashes ID and F, drives io_imemAddr = the
missing pc, waits for io_imemReady, writes {1, tag, io_imemData} into the
store and restarts fetch at that pc (the word is then read back through
the BSRAM, so ID has a single instruction source). io_imemReady therefore
only reaches the refill FSM flops; imem_stall leaves stall_if / kill_id.
Steering stays where it is (raw pre-decode + pc_d+B-imm / pc_d+J-imm adders
+ PHT in the ID cycle, pred_taken folded into redir_c1/redir_c0); the
adders now start at pc_d flops (no fa mux), and the next address
na = flush_q ? flush_pc_q : pred_taken ? tgt : pc_f+1 (hold when ID does
not advance, via the BSRAM CE so the output register holds too) drives
pc_f and the BSRAM address pins. A followed JAL / predicted-taken branch
squashes the one sequential word in F (valid bit f_v cleared, 1 bubble); a
redirect squashes ID and F (flush_q already kills the instruction in EX).
Index the PHT with pc_d (flops) so it is no longer behind the fa mux.
Cycle model (N ~3.0M, R ~0.13-0.14M redirects, ~0.27M followed taken
transfers, ~0.26M blocked cycles): today 4.28M; new ~= N + 0.27M (taken
bubble) + 3*R (redirect penalty 1 -> 3) + 0.26M ~= 3.95-4.0M with ID
steering, i.e. +7-8% iter/cycle, and no path gains a level: ID starts at a
register as it does now (LFSR flop in the bench), the bus is one flop-gated
load. If timing allows, the implementer should then recover the taken
bubble (-0.27M cycles, total ~+15%) as a second step only: store the
pre-decoded 30-bit target + {is_jal_ok, is_br_ok} at refill, read the
store in bypass mode into an explicit IF/ID flop and steer in F
(BSRAM dout -> 2 LUTs -> address pins). Ship step one first.
Correctness notes: tag is the full pc[31:13] so formal's symbolic pcs never
alias; riscv-formal has no imem-consistency check and its insn stream is
whatever the core reports, while cosim's program is immutable (no stores
into .text in bench/programs; confirm with the disassembly), so a stale
entry cannot occur; liveness holds because a miss always ends in a bus
fetch. RVFI insn/pc come from the same ID/EX fields as before. If the
inferred memory makes formal slow, shrink ENTRIES by parameter for formal
only via the existing `ifdef RISCV_FORMAL style used in muldiv.sv.

Fmax vs a same-session baseline, worst path (watch tgt/pred_taken -> BSRAM
address pins; if it is worst, register na in a flop pc_f and accept
redirect/taken penalties of +1 only after measuring).

~3.54M cycles by arithmetic), so compare the two before choosing which to re-port; evidence limits: the implementer timed placement option 0 only and no same-session baseline (sibling sessions read 113.3 / 117.5 / 117.5 for this base, so the loss is -3.7% same-option but -7.2% on the scored median, and this RTL's per-option numbers are unknown), and the hit rate was not instrumented (the cycle count matching the miss-free model is the only evidence that conflict misses are negligible); its notes did not reach this record).

title: Next-instruction predictor: PC-indexed successor-word table read beside the PHT and registered a cycle ahead, so a hit needs no imem bus (hides the 22% iStall)
motivation:
LESSONS closes the classic predictor budget: after JAL-follow + bimodal only
~55k redirect bubbles (1.3% of 4,281,466 cycles) are left, RAS measured +0.30%,
r4s2's next-line BTB gained no cycles, so direction/target accuracy can never
clear the +4.6% bar. The one large pool no logged experiment has touched is
the imem bus itself: io_imemReady is low ~22% of cycles and every such cycle
in which the back end could accept is a bubble (kill_id = load_use |
imem_stall). Rough split of the 4.28M cycles (estimate, not a trace):
~2.9M instructions x 1.28 (geometric wait for a ready cycle) + ~0.5M back-end
stall cycles + redirects, i.e. ~0.8M cycles (~19%) are pure iStall bubbles.
The four fetch-buffer builds only recovered ready cycles wasted under
back-end stalls (+6%) and each paid ~6% Fmax. A fetch-side table that
PREDICTS THE NEXT FETCHED WORD from the current fetch PC (a branch-target-
instruction cache generalised to every successor, looked up next to the PHT)
supplies the instruction from flops, so the bus is not needed on a hit:
100% hits would be ~3.46M cycles (+24% iter/cycle), 80% ~3.63M (+18%),
50% ~3.87M (+10.6%). Break-even Fmax loss is 10-15%, not the ~6% of the
fetch buffers. ARCHITECTURE.md counts "logic that handles or hides stalls"
as legal timed logic; test/cosim/main.cpp and fpga/bench_stall_gen.sv draw
the ready bits independently of the address, and imem_data / imem_ready are
flops in the timed wrapper (core_bench_si.sv), so the head mux below starts
at flops on both legs.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a direct-mapped next-instruction table (NIT) to if_stage, indexed and
tagged by the CURRENT fetch PC P and holding the word of P's successor:
  entry[P[AW-1:0]] = { tag = P[29:AW], dir, word }   (LUT-RAM, async read,
  syn_ramstyle="distributed_ram"; valid = 2^AW RESET flops like
  reg_file.written - correctness-critical, unlike the PHT)
dir = the stored successor was reached by a fetch-followed taken transfer
(pred_taken) vs sequentially. Program text is immutable and the successor
address is a static function of (P, dir) (P+4, or P + B/J-imm of the word at
P), so with the full tag a hit is EXACT: no verify, no EX logic, no new
redirect, wrong-path words are still the right word for their address.
pc_q / tgt / fa_inc / PHT / flush_q logic is untouched.

Lookup (cycle N, fetching P), flops only: idx = pc_q[AW-1:0],
t_hit = valid[idx] && tag[idx] == pc_q[29:AW]. Registered result:
  nb_instr_q <= stall ? cur_instr  : t_word
  nb_v_q     <= stall ? have_instr : (t_hit && !flush_q && t_dir == pred_taken)
(next state precomputed stall-free, stall only the final 2:1 select - r6s2
lesson; pred_taken gets ONE new flop sink; EX's late `redirect` gets none).
Use (cycle N+1), selects are flops:
  use_nb     = nb_v_q && !flush_q        // the flush cycle fetches another pc
  cur_instr  = use_nb ? nb_instr_q : imem_data      // one LUT4 per bit
  have_instr = use_nb || imem_ready
  imem_stall = !have_instr               // hazard_unit: replaces !imem_ready
The stall branch doubles as a 1-word skid: a word the bus delivered while the
back end stalled (dmem / load-use / ex_busy) is kept, so the retry does not
need a second ready cycle (part of the fetch-buffer gain, no queue).
Fill, flop-sourced, independent of stall: every cycle prev_fa_q <= fa,
prev_tk_q <= pred_taken, adv_q <= !stall; when adv_q && !flush_q &&
imem_ready && !nb_v_q write entry[prev_fa_q] = {tag, prev_tk_q, imem_data}
and set valid. A branch keeps its last direction's successor.

Order of work (budget is tight; r5s2's 4-entry LUT-RAM instruction queue died
on a 2700 s formal timeout in `causal`, so formal goes FIRST):
1. Build with parameter AW=6 (64 x 57 bit, ~60 RAM16 + 64 valid flops), run
   RTL_DIR=cores/bench/rtl CORE_NAME=bench bash formal/run_all.sh and
   NRET=1 make cosim TARGET=bench. The formal wrapper ties imemReady=1 and
   makes imem_data symbolic per cycle; a table word is just another legal
   stream and rvfi_insn is the executed word, so no check needs touching.
   If formal wall time grows badly, shrink AW (4/5) before anything else.
2. CoreMark cycles at AW=6, then AW=7 / 8 if formal headroom allows; keep
   the best cycles x median Fmax over all three placement options against a
   same-session baseline. Record cycles, per-option Fmax, worst path.
3. Timing: B/J immediates are pure wiring from the word, so the head mux only
   makes the word side of the target adders arrive level with `fa` (1 LUT);
   op_br/op_jal still precede the PHT bit. Paths that do gain a level:
   word -> load-use compare -> stall_if and word -> regfile read address.
   If one enters the top 5: (a) run the load-use compares on nb_instr_q and
   imem_data in parallel and select with use_nb after them; (b) register the
   nb word's load-use flag a cycle ahead (nb_lu_q <= stall ? (dmem_stall &&
   load_use) : P is a LOAD with rd != 0 equal to t_word rs1/rs2) and its
   op_jal/op_br/alignment pre-decode bits, so hits start from flops. Never
   index the table by `fa` (keeps flush_q -> fa off the RAM read).
Expected: 3.6-3.9M cycles (+10..18% iter/cycle) for -4..-9% Fmax.
Risks, in order: formal runtime with the extra memory; unmeasured hit rate
of a small direct-mapped table on CoreMark's hot set (list/matrix/crc loops
fit, the state switch and call chains alias; taken transfers alternate);
diffuse LUT-RAM area/routing cost; self-modifying code is unsupported
(none in the bench programs; clear valid on FENCE if a test needs it).

implementation_notes:
# Next-instruction table (NIT) — implementation notes

## What was changed

`rtl/if_stage.sv`
- New parameter `AW` (shipped: **8**, 256 entries) and a direct-mapped
  next-instruction table: LUT-RAM `nit[2^AW] = {tag = P[29:AW], dir, word}`
  (async read, `syn_ramstyle = "distributed_ram"`) plus `2^AW` reset valid
  flops. Indexed/tagged by the CURRENT fetch pc `pc_q` (never by `fa`), holds
  the word of that pc's successor and the direction it was reached by.
- Registered a cycle ahead: `nb_instr_q <= stall ? cur_instr : t_word`,
  `nb_v_q <= stall ? have_instr : (t_hit && !flush && t_dir == pred_taken)`
  (stall is only the final 2:1 select; the stall leg is the 1-word skid).
- Head mux `cur_instr = use_nb ? nb_instr_q : imem_data` feeds pre-decode,
  target adders and `out.instr`; `have_instr = use_nb || imem_ready` is exported.
- Fill from flops: `prev_fa_q / prev_tk_q / adv_q`, write when
  `adv_q && !flush && imem_ready && !nb_v_q`.
- New inputs `imem_ready`, `flush_nb_q`; new output `have_instr`.
  pc_q / PHT / target adders / flush logic are structurally untouched.

`rtl/hazard_unit.sv`: `imem_stall = !have_instr` (port renamed from `imem_ready`).

`rtl/ex_stage.sv`: one extra flop `flush_dup_q` (`syn_preserve`), same D input
as `flush_q`, exported as `flush_nb_q`. It is logically identical to `flush_q`
and is used only by the NIT logic in IF.

`rtl/core.sv`: wiring only.

`test/test_next_instr_table.py`: (1) loop with an alternating branch, JAL,
load-use and stores vs a Python model with no / imem / dmem / both stalls
(POISON store on the bus when not ready); (2) a warm tight loop keeps
retiring (>= 100 instructions) with the imem bus held not-ready. Passes.

## Deviations from the plan

- **Duplicate flush flop** (not in the plan). The first build (AW=6) had
  `flush_q` (fanout 107, 1.6 ns net) -> head mux -> load-use compare -> stall
  as its worst path. `use_nb = nb_v_q && !flush_nb_q` now takes a dedicated
  copy. Measured effect was small (p0 104.0 -> median 104.7 at AW=6), and at
  AW=7/8 the copy's own D path (EX compare -> flush_dup_q) shows up as worst
  path on placement options 1/2.
- **AW=8 instead of 6** — chosen from the measurements below.
- Timing options (a)/(b) of the plan (parallel load-use compares, registered
  nb load-use / pre-decode bits) were NOT implemented: no time left.
- No FENCE invalidation of the table (self-modifying code unsupported, as in
  the plan).

## Measurements (this session, vendor flow, 3 placement options)

Baseline RTL rebuilt in this session: Fmax [113.319, 117.497, 117.497],
median 117.497 MHz, LUT 2801 / FF 835 / LUT-RAM 64. Baseline CoreMark cycles
were NOT re-run here; 4,281,466 is the figure from the hypothesis text.

| build                         | CoreMark cycles | Fmax p0 / p1 / p2 (MHz)     | median  | LUT / FF / LUT-RAM |
|-------------------------------|-----------------|-----------------------------|---------|--------------------|
| AW=5                          | 3,758,524       | not built                   | -       | -                  |
| AW=6, no dup flop             | 3,696,899       | 104.0 / - / -               | -       | 3487 / 964 / 124   |
| AW=6                          | 3,696,899       | 96.263 / 104.677 / 104.677  | 104.677 | 3493 / 965 / 124   |
| AW=7                          | 3,605,837       | 103.386 / 105.586 / 105.586 | 105.586 | 4033 / 1029 / 176  |
| **AW=8 (shipped)**            | **3,536,081**   | 88.016 / 104.995 / 104.995  | 104.995 | 5139 / 1157 / 288  |
| AW=8, 18-bit tag (rejected)   | 3,536,081       | 82.791 / 93.637 / 93.637    | 93.637  | 4735 / 1157 / 240  |
| AW=8, 18-bit tag, no dup, bubble on flush (rejected) | 3,574,871 | 81.645 / 92.252 / 92.252 | 92.252 | 4740 / 1156 / 240 |

(Cycle counts for AW=5/6/7 were taken before the duplicate flop was added;
it does not change behaviour. The AW=8 count was re-measured on the final RTL.)

Estimated fitness vs baseline, using 4,281,466 baseline cycles:
AW=6 +3.2 %, AW=7 +6.7 %, **AW=8 +8.2 %** (Fmax -10.6 %, cycles -17.4 %).

Worst paths of the shipped build:
- option 0 (88.0 MHz): `u_if/pc_q` -> NIT RAM read -> 22-bit tag compare -> `u_if/nb_v_q` (31 cells)
- options 1/2 (105.0 MHz): `u_mem/reg_q.rd_val` -> EX compare -> redirect -> `u_ex/flush_dup_q` (38 cells)

## Concerns

- The score rests on placement options 1 and 2 (identical results); option 0
  is an 88 MHz outlier. Fmax is very placement-sensitive here: narrowing the
  stored tag to pc[17:AW] (smaller RAM, shorter compare) made every option
  ~11 % slower, so small RTL edits can move the result a lot.
- Fmax loss (-10.6 %) is at the upper end of the hypothesis' expectation
  (-4..-9 %); the head mux puts one more level on word -> load-use -> stall and
  word -> regfile read address, exactly as predicted. The registered
  pre-decode / load-use flag (plan option b) is the obvious follow-up.
- Area +83 % LUT (2801 -> 5139), mostly the 256 x 55 LUT-RAM and its read mux.
- Correctness relies on program text being immutable and imem data being a
  pure function of the address. The table is never invalidated.
- Fill only happens when the bus is ready in the first cycle after an advance
  (`adv_q`), as specified; a held "pending fill" would raise the hit rate a
  little but needs `stall` on 31 more flop enables.
- Process note: the first batch of RTL edits was applied with an inline
  `python3 - <<EOF` from the shell (it only rewrote cores/bench/rtl files and
  left no script behind); later edits used the edit tool. Scratch builds lived
  in $TMPDIR / .tmp only.

## Local check status

- verilator lint: clean.
- cosim (`NRET=1 make cosim TARGET=bench`) on the final RTL: passed
  (selftest + CoreMark, CRCs valid, "Correct operation validated", oob false).
- cocotb: full `cores/bench/test` suite passes on the final RTL (8 runner
  tests, including the new `test_next_instr_table.py`).
- formal (`formal/run_all.sh`):
  - AW=6, full tag, no dup flop: **PASS**, 7m08s wall (reg_ch0 427 s is the
    long pole; causal / liveness 4 s each) on a loaded host.
  - final RTL (AW=8, full tag, dup flop): **PASS on the first attempt**,
    53 passed / 0 failed, 3m30s wall. No fix attempts were needed.
  - A run on the rejected 18-bit-tag variant was stopped early and never
    completed; it says nothing about that variant.

title: Forwarding-free EX: EX result captured into ID/EX operands, regfile written at MEM, registered PHT read
motivation:
The champion (130.22 MHz, 4,283,613 cycles, 304.00) is limited on placement
options 1/2 by four families within 5 ps at 7.68 ns: the add/sub carry
(ID/EX.alu_sub -> alu_result[26], 31 cells), fwd_a_ex -> alu_result (8 cells),
imem_data -> op_a/op_b D (7-9 cells) and pc_q -> PHT -> pc_q (10 cells);
option 0 sits on EX/MEM.alu_result -> forward mux -> compare -> flush_q.
LESSONS says everything IPC-side that is not a fetch buffer / early load sums
to <= 3.5% and is unacceptable, and that the only two accepted changes since
r1 (r4s1, r7s0) were RELOCATIONS of a late mux onto a register D input, timed
family by family. Three forwarding / lookup muxes still sit at the HEAD of the
critical loops and each one can be relocated or deleted with zero cycle cost:
  (1) the EX/MEM forward mux in front of ALU, shifter, compare, address adder;
  (2) the regfile write-first (WB) bypass mux behind the LUT-RAM read in ID;
  (3) the async 512-entry PHT mux tree between pc_q and the pc_q D input.
This is the same recipe as r7s0 (MEM/WB leg -> ID/EX D inputs, +10.8%) applied
to the legs r7s0 left in place, all in one change as r4s0's lesson requires.
